US President Donald Trump said he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran and that “you’ll know soon enough.” “Now we’ll make a decision: Do we want to go further and just certify it, by certifying it meaning it will never happen again?” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. And you’ll know soon enough,” he said. Trump also dismissed speculation that he is considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, stating that “he’s doing a very good job.” - Turkish parliament approves Mecca joint defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia The Turkish parliament approved a bill ratifying the Mecca Agreement on Joint Defense between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, clearing the way for the trilateral security pact to take effect. Lawmakers endorsed the measure by 279 votes to 119, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 members taking part in the ballot. During the debate, ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party lawmaker Ziya Altunyaldiz stressed that the agreement aims to expand security cooperation in the region. He emphasized that it contains no approach against any third country and that its main goal is to prevent conflicts rather than escalate them. - Israel's president to announce Sunday who will be tasked with forming government Israel’s president said he will announce Sunday which lawmaker will be tasked with forming the next government following consultations with political parties following last month’s elections. In a Thursday video message reported by Israeli news outlet Ynet, Isaac Herzog said parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, while parties holding 46 seats backed current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party. “The results of the consultations may appear clear,” Herzog said, but added that the ability to form a government remains uncertain due to mutual objections between and within political blocs. He said he would hold further individual talks with party leaders to assess their prospects of forming a coalition. Herzog stressed that he would make every effort to facilitate the formation of a stable government. ... - French authorities reported more than 400 arrests and over 50 injured police officers as hundreds of thousands of people joined nationwide protests over wages and the rising cost of living.

items.excerpt: NEW YORK (AP) — A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centers. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% Thursday for its worst drop since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The wipeout more than erased the market’s gain from the day before, which was its best in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,800 points, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%. AI stocks worldwide felt pressure as worries rise about possible moratoriums on data centers following Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections. ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay (AP) — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is under criminal investigation following the collapse of a major digital bank, as the South American leader prepares to defend himself before the Senate against possible removal from office on Friday. The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist. In a day of lightning-speed developments, Peña offered his resignation Thursday, with the lower house voting unanimously to impeach him moments later. Both houses declined to accept Peña’s offer to resign, with the Senate instead deciding to press forward with a trial that could result in the president’s removal from office.

The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 5.5% on Thursday, wiping an estimated $2.5 trillion from its market value and entering correction territory. Nvidia lost more than 9%, while semiconductor stocks suffered even steeper declines. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress after campaigns that included opposition to rapid data centre expansion. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new approvals. Investors were already questioning whether enormous spending on AI infrastructure would generate expected returns, while tighter approvals could delay projects and increase costs. The sell-off spread into Asian markets on Friday. Japan’s Nikkei fell 6% in early trading, South Korea’s Kospi dropped more than 8.5%, triggering a trading halt and Taiwan’s Taiex lost over 8.3%. The S&P 500 also fell 4.4%. ###### Sources: BBC, Wall Street Journal Republicans’ sweeping midterm defeat has thrown the party’s 2028 presidential succession into uncertainty, with Vice President JD Vance distancing himself from President Donald Trump’s Iran war and potential rivals positioning themselves for a contest. Vance blamed the war for the losses, calling for an end to the conflict, greater attention to affordability and a reassessment of US relations with Israel. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the result as an “extinction-level event” for Republicans, while Senator Ted Cruz criticised the war’s duration and the party’s failure to address voters’ economic concerns. Vance remains the nomination front-runner, supported by influential donors and conservative organisations but Trump’s endorsement has not materialised. Meanwhile, Democrats’ capture of both congressional chambers gives them greater scope to challenge the administration’s war policy through funding restrictions and investigations. The defeat has intensified debate over the party’s direction beyond Trump. Iran and the United States are reviewing nuclear proposals through Qatari mediation, signalling renewed diplomatic engagement as both sides weigh the risk of further military escalation. A senior Iranian official said Tehran had submitted a proposal to Washington, while other officials described discussions of concrete terms for Iran’s nuclear programme. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei publicly maintained that negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz depend on Washington meeting seven demands, including sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets. Privately, however, officials said he had shown greater willingness to discuss nuclear issues. US Vice President JD Vance has supported the mediation effort, while President Donald Trump has retained the option of renewed strikes. Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains a central obstacle, with Tehran opposing its removal from the country. The diplomatic activity follows weeks of confrontation and warnings of wider regional retaliation. Saudi Arabia faces mounting military and diplomatic difficulties as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis intensify attacks on its oil facilities and airports while advancing towards Aden, the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The militants reportedly demanded $51 billion and recognition as Yemen’s rulers in return for ending hostilities, although Saudi Deputy Minister Rayed Krimly denied that any financial demand had been made. The Houthis have moved within roughly 50 miles of Aden, while repeated strikes on Saudi infrastructure have disrupted travel and damaged energy facilities. Saudi airstrikes have failed to halt their advance, and deploying ground forces risks heavy casualties. Riyadh’s options are further constrained by limited allied support. The United Arab Emirates has withdrawn from the campaign, while Pakistan and Egypt have ruled out offensive operations. Any settlement involving payments could also establish a precedent for further demands, leaving Saudi Arabia facing prolonged insecurity or costly military escalation. Israeli President Isaac Herzog will decide on Sunday who should attempt to form a government after opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot secured 67 parliamentary recommendations, compared with 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Neither bloc won a majority in the October election, leaving the country’s political future dependent on difficult coalition negotiations. ... Hundreds of thousands ... Nearly 90 million forcibly displaced people, about three-quarters of the global total, live in countries highly exposed to drought, flooding and extreme heat, the UN refugee agency said ahead of COP31 in Turkey. The agency warned that climate hazards are compounding the difficulties facing people displaced by conflict and persecution.

items.title: Markets fret over growth and inflation despite easing oil prices By Reuters
items.excerpt: LONDON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Uncertainty over the growth outlook and expectations that inflation will remain elevated next year are weighing on global markets, even as hopes of a de-escalation in the Iran war have eased oil prices. Government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year, the tech-led Nasdaq racked up on Thursday its biggest one-day drop since April 2025’s Liberation Day rout and European economic data has softened. The combination is fuelling concern that inflation could stay high even as growth slows, although the Democratic victory in US midterm elections has raised hopes for an eventual end to the Iran war. OIL STILL HIGH Oil has fallen 15% this week to just below $100 a barrel. But analysts warn that any resolution to the Iran war remains uncertain, leaving scope for prices to rise again. Oil is still up 64% this year, while natural gas remains nearly three times its level at the start of 2026. That backdrop is keeping near-term inflation expectations elevated and reinforcing concerns that price pressures could persist as growth slows, forcing central banks to raise interest rates further. The University of Michigan’s measure of one-year US inflation expectations edged up to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in September and ​3.4% in February. Market measures of long-term inflation expectations remain above 2% in the euro zone and the US, and above 3% in Britain. Higher energy costs add to inflation while also weighing on growth by increasing transport, manufacturing and household expenses.

items.title: US job growth expected to pick up in October, with moderation in wage gains By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 06, 2026, 12:04 AM Updated Nov 06, 2026, 12:48 AM ... By Lucia Mutikani WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US nonfarm payrolls likely picked up in October, but an anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3.0% for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years would reinforce the view that the labor market was not a source of inflation. The Labor Department’s closely watched employment report on Friday is also expected to show the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.2% last month, with a high probability it may have slipped to 4.1%. Historically low layoffs and a recent jump in job openings have raised the prospect of labor market tightening. But economists and Federal Reserve officials have maintained that the labor market poses no inflation risk. Some economists have argued that a shrinking supply of workers amid an immigration crackdown and retirements is the primary driver of the relatively low unemployment rate. "We have got a jobs market which isn’t generating wage growth in any meaningful way. That really should help to dampen medium-term price pressures because the biggest cost input for corporate America is labor," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING. "Weak wage growth should the give Fed some confidence that over the medium term, inflation will continue trending towards target." Nonfarm payrolls likely increased by 65,000 jobs last month, a Reuters survey of economists predicted, after being restricted to a 29,000 gain in September because of a calendar quirk related to a late Labor Day holiday. Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs. October payrolls could also miss expectations, with some economists noting seasonal factors, used by the government to strip out seasonal fluctuations from the data, were unfavorable for the month. Employment gains have averaged 68,000 jobs per month this year. Economists say the economy needs to create at least 40,000 per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called breakeven rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labor force. Payroll gains have lagged economic growth, with gross domestic product increasing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, fueled by strong consumer spending and businesses aggressively investing in artificial intelligence. Economists said employers likely overhired after the COVID pandemic, and some businesses were probably uncertain about their staffing needs as they incorporated AI into their operations. They said uncertainty stemming from the US-Israel war with Iran, which has raised energy prices, was also making employers hesitant to increase headcount. Limited opportunities have made job hopping harder, curbing wage growth. ... Average hourly earnings are forecast to have increased 0.3% in October after edging up 0.1% in September. Wages are expected to have advanced 2.9% in the 12 months through October. That would be the first year-on-year increase below 3% since May 2021 and a slowdown from a 3.0% gain in September. While that would highlight the disinflationary impulse from the labor market, it would illustrate the further erosion of household incomes, already pressured by inflation. Income at the disposal of households after adjusting for inflation and taxes fell in September. Economists expect consumer spending and the broader economy will slow down in the fourth quarter and into 2027. They continued to expect the US central bank to raise interest rates in December, though some believed benign wage pressure could limit the number of rate hikes next year. The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Next Tuesday’s consumer inflation report for October could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027. "The labor market is not too hot, not too cold," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "So, the Fed has nothing to worry about when it comes to the labor situation."

items.title: Hammack Favors Smaller Fed Moves as Inflation Stays Above Target | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 6, 2026, 2:12 AM UTC Updated Nov 6, 2026, 2:12 AM UTC 2 min read ... A nearly six-year stretch of inflation above the Federal Reserve’s 2% goal is shaping Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack’s support for measured adjustments, even as she expects monetary policy to become restrictive. At the SNB and Its Watchers Conference in Zurich on Thursday, Nov. 5, Hammack said smaller changes made more frequently could be preferable when conditions permit. She argued that this approach could ease disruption for households, businesses and financial markets. She also said it could reduce the chance that policymakers fall behind price pressures and allow an inflationary mindset to take hold. Hammack did not give a date or size for future policy adjustments in her prepared remarks. “I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance,” she said. She added that the speech reflected her own views, not necessarily those of the Federal Reserve System or her colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September. The core measure, which excludes food and energy, increased 3.1%. Hammack described inflation pressures as broad-based, with contributions from both supply and demand, and said inflation had exceeded the Fed’s goal for nearly six years. The FOMC voted 10-2 on Oct. 28 to keep the federal funds target range at 3.75%-4.00%. Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook preferred a 0.25-percentage-point increase. Hammack had previously said policy would need to become restrictive, as detailed in EconoTimes’ earlier report on her policy outlook. The BEA’s next Personal Income and Outlays report, covering October and including the PCE index, is scheduled for Nov. 25 at 8:30 a.m. EST. The FOMC’s next meeting is set for Dec. 8-9.

items.title: 2026 midterm election live updates as Democrats flip over 40 House seats, GOP grapples with stunning losses
items.excerpt: ## Latest updates on 2026 midterm election results: - After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, Democratic leaders are laying out how they plan to wield power with President Trump in the White House while Republicans are preparing for their time in the minority. - Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats after upsets in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and more. The Alaska and Mississippi races remain unresolved. - House Democrats are on track to control around 256 seats, CBS News estimates, after flipping more than 40 districts — some of which were viewed as deep-red — and staving off major losses from redistricting. - In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, won the highly watched mayor's race, defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, CBS News projects. - Find updates on key House races here, Senate battleground races here and all election results in the CBS News Election Center. ... ## Judge blocks DOJ from demanding election workers in Washington reject certain ballots U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead granted a temporary restraining order blocking the Justice Department from demanding that election workers in Washington state reject ballots of voters suspected of being noncitizens. The department was also barred from threatening workers with prosecution if they don't comply. "Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claim that Defendants have exceeded their authority, and the harm to Washington voters whose ballots are set aside on the strength of an unreliable federal list cannot be undone after the fact," Whitehead wrote in the ruling, which came in a lawsuit filed by several groups. Prior to Election Day, the Justice Department pushed officials in multiple states to crack down on alleged voting by non-citizens. Federal prosecutors in Washington asked the state's top election official last week to set aside ballots from more than 400 people who they believe aren't citizens. State officials responded that "many of the persons on your list are United States citizens" and a "significant number" aren't registered to vote in the state.

items.title: Republicans rammed through Supreme Court nominees. Now Democrats will have the votes to stop them
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump led a transformation of the Supreme Court that ushered in a conservative supermajority but soon he will confront an emboldened Democratic-led Senate that is preparing to play hardball on his judicial nominations. items.title: Trump arch construction blocked after federal approval : NPR
items.excerpt: A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately. Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia. She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion, in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery. ### Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions. "The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed. Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure. The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge. A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.

items.title: White House denies Hegseth, Rubio will leave jobs amid Republican election fallout
items.excerpt: The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration. US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses. One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." ## Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run. Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview. "I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'" The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news". The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future. Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate. In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him. Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth ... Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.

items.title: Lil Baby & JENNIE Lead Best New Music: Friday Music Guide
items.excerpt: Billboard’s Friday Music Guide serves as a handy guide to New Music Friday’s most essential releases each week — the key music that everyone will be talking about today, and that will be dominating playlists this weekend and beyond. This week, Lil Baby is back with his anticipated fifth album; JENNIE drops a new single for the animated Netflix film STEPS; Dove Cameron releases her long-awaited debut album; and Boys Noize returns with his first solo studio album in five years.… plus much more. Check out all of this week’s picks below: Lil Baby, Fresh After scoring his third consecutive Billboard 200 No. 1 album with WHAM last year, Lil Baby is gunning for his fourth with Fresh. The new set arrives with a title inspired by his recent hit single “Dead Fresh,” an infectious, Pharrell-produced joint that soared to No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped Rhythmic Airplay. Stacked with guest appearances by frequent collaborators Future, Young Thug and Rylo Rodriguez, Fresh finds Baby delivering 17 new songs that reassert his position as one of the most gifted mainstream MCs to blow up this decade. — KYLE DENIS JENNIE, “Someone To Hold” The inviting disco-colored intro of “Someone To Hold” neither sounds like a typical song for JENNIE nor a Disney princess — and that’s what makes it magic. The colorful pop song shows a new side of JENNIE’s artistry that leans more playful and vibrant than anything on her solo debut full-length, while also matching the fresh take of the movie it’s from — as the upcoming musical comedy Steps reimagines Cinderella from the perspective of the stepsisters. — L.H. Dove Cameron, Final Girl Despite launching her career over a decade ago in Disney TV and film franchises — also lending her voice to both — Final Girl is Dove Cameron’s debut full-length. At long last. The dramatic and soaring album delivers a range of tempos and emotions, from softer songs like pop ballad “Silver Screen Baby” and the raw “Immortalized” to uptempo dance-pop single “When In Rome” and the haunting and heavy “Skin On Bone.” It’s an album that was well worth the wait, and offers so much possibility and intrigue as to what sounds and styles Cameron will want to explore next. — L.H. Kings Of Leon, “Rose” Veteran rock band Kings Of Leon has released its 10th album, O My Beloved — and the first the band has ever self-produced. ... XG, “Depends”

items.excerpt: ## Ramayana Box Office Collection Day 1 As per Sacnilk, Ramayana opened at Rs. 64.85 crore net across all languages in India, while its first-day gross collection stood at Rs. 77.50 crore. The film was expected to make a bigger impact at the box office, with trade expectations suggesting that its opening-day net earnings could cross the Rs. 80 crore mark. However, the actual figures fell short of that target. Released in five languages — Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada — the film recorded its highest collection from the Hindi version. It earned Rs. 47.50 crore net in Hindi alone. The Kannada version came second with Rs. 7.25 crore, despite expectations of a stronger opening, especially with Yash playing Ravana. Meanwhile, the Telugu version collected Rs. 6 crore, followed by Tamil with Rs. 2.60 crore and Malayalam with Rs. 1.50 crore net on its opening day. ... ## Who Will Win Rise And Fall 2 Finale Today? After weeks of drama, heated arguments, unexpected twists, and emotional moments, Rise And Fall 2 will conclude with its grand finale today (November 6). Only six contestants are now left in the race for the Rise And Fall 2 winner's trophy and prize money. Shehzad Poonawalla, Gautam Gulati, Priyanka Chahar Chaudhary, Swara Bhasker, Karan Patel, and Niharika Tiwari have secured their places in the finale. However, only one of them will emerge as the winner.
